meta.blurb: When their father dies, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood lose their home and most of their money. One sister hides her feelings, and the other shows every one. Two broken hearts, one cruel secret and a very long, wet walk will teach them what sense and sensibility are worth.
meta.bible: Elinor Dashwood: nineteen at the start; sensible, calm and loyal; hides her feelings to protect others; loves Edward Ferrars. Marianne Dashwood: sixteen at the start; passionate, romantic and honest about every feeling; falls in love with Willoughby. Margaret Dashwood: the youngest sister, thirteen, cheerful and imaginative. Mrs Dashwood: their warm, romantic mother, who is as quick to feel as Marianne. Mr Henry Dashwood: their father, who dies in the first beat and leaves them little. John Dashwood: Mr Henry Dashwood's son by his first wife; the half brother of the sisters; weak and easily led. Fanny Dashwood: John's wife, selfish and proud, who persuades him to give nothing; sister of Edward and Robert Ferrars. Edward Ferrars: Fanny's brother; shy, kind and honest; secretly engaged to Lucy Steele. Robert Ferrars: Edward's younger brother, vain and silly. Mrs Ferrars: their rich, domineering mother. Sir John Middleton: a cheerful, generous cousin who owns Barton Park and lets the Dashwoods a cottage. Lady Middleton: his cold, polite wife. Mrs Jennings: her loud, warm and meddling mother, who loves matchmaking. Colonel Brandon: about thirty-five, a quiet, loyal soldier who loves Marianne; he owns Delaford. John Willoughby: a handsome, charming young man who woos Marianne and then drops her for a rich bride, Miss Grey. Mrs Smith: Willoughby's rich old aunt, who lives at Allenham. Eliza Williams: a girl whom Willoughby ruined and abandoned; Colonel Brandon's ward and the daughter of his first love. Lucy Steele and Anne Steele: sisters, cousins of Mrs Jennings; Lucy is sly and clever and is secretly engaged to Edward. Mr and Mrs Palmer: Mrs Jennings's other daughter, Charlotte, and her husband, who own Cleveland. Places: Norland Park in Sussex, the Dashwoods' old home; Barton Cottage and Barton Park in Devonshire; Allenham; Whitwell; Exeter; London; Cleveland in Somerset; Delaford, the Colonel's parsonage and estate. Voice and tone: warm, ironic and clear; the sisters are different but both are right in some things and wrong in others; the book ends happily and fairly.

B1B2: Mr Henry Dashwood had owned Norland Park, but he fell ill and knew that he would soon die. He asked his son John to look after his second wife and their three daughters, and John promised that he would.
John first thought that he should give his stepsisters three thousand pounds, which was a generous gift. His wife Fanny argued with him until he decided that a few small favours would be enough.

Elinor, the eldest, was calm, careful and sensible, and she always thought before she spoke. Marianne, who was sixteen, was lively, romantic and honest about every feeling, and she could not hide her joy or her sorrow.
Soon after the funeral, Fanny and John moved into Norland Park with their little son. Fanny behaved as if the house were already hers, and she spoke coldly to Mrs Dashwood, who felt deeply hurt.
Fanny's brother Edward Ferrars visited Norland and soon became Elinor's close friend. He was shy and not especially handsome, but he was kind and honest, and Elinor admired him.
One day Mrs Dashwood received a kind letter from her cousin Sir John Middleton, who lived in Devonshire. He offered her a small cottage near his own house, and she gladly accepted at once.
The Dashwoods said goodbye to Norland with tears and travelled to Barton Cottage in Devonshire. The cottage was small and a little damp, but the valley around it was green and beautiful.

Sir John Middleton was a cheerful, generous man who loved visitors, and he welcomed the Dashwoods warmly. At his home, they met his quiet wife and her mother, Mrs Jennings, who laughed a great deal and loved to match young people.

At Barton Park they also met Colonel Brandon, a quiet and serious man of about thirty-five. He listened to Marianne's playing with great attention, and Marianne thought that he was far too old for love.
One rainy day, Marianne ran down a hill and twisted her ankle in the wet grass. A handsome young man with a gun and two dogs picked her up and carried her all the way to the cottage.
Willoughby came to the cottage every day to ask about Marianne's ankle. They discovered that they loved the same books, the same songs and the same dances, and they talked for hours.
Willoughby asked for a lock of Marianne's hair, and she gave it with a smile. Elinor felt that this was too open, because they had not said that they were engaged.
Elinor asked her mother whether Marianne and Willoughby were engaged, because they had never said so. Mrs Dashwood said she believed that they loved each other and that questions would be unkind.

Willoughby and Marianne laughed at Colonel Brandon's gentle manners and his love of quiet, but Elinor defended him. She said that he was an excellent and well-informed man, and that Marianne was being unfair.
Willoughby offered to give Marianne a fine horse of her own. Elinor pointed out that they were poor and could not keep a horse, and that she should not take such a gift from him.
The neighbours planned a day out to Whitwell, the Colonel's estate, but a letter arrived that morning. Colonel Brandon turned pale and left at once, and he would not say why he had to go.

Willoughby took Marianne to see Allenham, the house of his rich aunt, Mrs Smith, and showed her every room. Elinor was shocked when she heard of it, because it seemed very improper for a young woman to do such a thing.

One morning, Willoughby came to the cottage looking very unhappy and said that he must go to London at once. His aunt had sent him on business, and he did not know when he would return, and Marianne wept for hours.
Edward Ferrars came to visit the cottage for a week, but he did not seem happy. Marianne noticed a ring on his finger with a lock of hair, and Edward grew red when she asked about it.
Edward left after only a week, and he seemed sorry to go. Elinor was disappointed, but she kept busy with her drawing and her work, because she did not wish to make her mother sad.
Mrs Jennings's two young cousins, Lucy and Anne Steele, came to stay at Barton Park. Lucy was clever and pretty, and she seemed especially keen to be friendly with Elinor.
One evening, Lucy told Elinor in secret that she had been engaged to Edward Ferrars for four years. She showed a small picture of Edward as proof, and Elinor felt as if her heart had stopped.
Elinor kept Lucy's secret, and she told nobody, not even her mother or her sister. At last she understood Edward's strange sadness, and she felt sorry for him, as well as for herself.
In the winter, Mrs Jennings invited Elinor and Marianne to stay with her in London. Marianne agreed with joy, because she hoped to see Willoughby there, and Elinor went to take care of her.
In London, Marianne wrote to Willoughby several times, and she waited for his answer each morning. No reply came, and she became more and more anxious, while Elinor watched and worried.
At a large party, Marianne saw Willoughby across the room, standing with a fashionable young lady. When she tried to speak to him, he answered with a cold bow, and she almost fainted.
Next morning, Willoughby sent back all her letters and the lock of hair, with a cold note saying he did not love her. Elinor learned that he was engaged to marry a rich young woman named Miss Grey.
Mrs Jennings tried to comfort Marianne with kind words, sweets and a glass of wine. Her loud and well-meant sympathy only made Marianne feel worse, but Elinor saw that her heart was good.
Colonel Brandon visited and told Elinor a sad story about Willoughby. Long ago the Colonel loved a girl who died, and her daughter Eliza came to him, but Willoughby ruined her life.
Elinor told Marianne what the Colonel had said, and Marianne listened in silence. She began to see that Willoughby had never been the man she thought, and that was a bitter lesson.
John and Fanny Dashwood came to London, and they were kind to the Steeles because they thought them people of position. Fanny knew nothing of Lucy's secret, and Elinor said nothing.

Anne Steele could not keep a secret, and she told Fanny that Lucy and Edward were engaged. Mrs Ferrars and Fanny were furious, and Fanny fell into hysterics, while poor Lucy was sent out of the house.
Mrs Ferrars called Edward and ordered him to give up Lucy, but he refused to break his promise. She was so angry that she cut him out of her will and gave his fortune to his brother Robert.

Colonel Brandon admired Edward's honesty, and he offered him the church at Delaford, which would give him a small income. Elinor, who loved Edward, agreed to give him the message, and she did so without crying.
In the spring, Elinor and Marianne left London and stopped at Cleveland, the home of Mr and Mrs Palmer, on the road home. Marianne, still sad, spent her time walking alone in the large garden.
One evening Marianne walked in the wet grass for a long time, thinking sadly about Willoughby. She came back wet and cold, and the next day she had a fever and a very sore throat.
Elinor nursed Marianne day and night, and the doctor feared that she was very sick. Colonel Brandon, who was visiting, rode through the night to bring Mrs Dashwood to her daughter's side.
In the middle of the night, Willoughby arrived at Cleveland, because he had heard that Marianne was dying. He told Elinor that he had loved Marianne truly, but he had been afraid to be poor.
At last Marianne's fever broke, and she slept peacefully, and the doctor said that she would live. Mrs Dashwood arrived soon after, and she wept with relief when she saw that her daughter was safe.
When Marianne was stronger, Elinor told her what Willoughby had said. Marianne wept, but she also saw that her own wild feelings had led her into danger, and she wished to change.

At Barton Cottage, Marianne decided to read for six hours a day and to practise her music, and she thanked Elinor for being so patient. She said that she would never again be ruled by her feelings alone.
One day, a servant came back from Exeter with surprising news: he had seen Edward Ferrars, and Mr Ferrars's new wife, Miss Steele. Elinor felt a great wave of sorrow, though she tried not to show it.
Soon afterward, Edward Ferrars himself rode to the cottage gate, and Elinor thought that she must be dreaming. He told them that Lucy had married his brother Robert, and that he himself was free.
When he found Elinor alone, Edward spoke to her honestly and asked her to marry him. She said yes, and she cried with happiness, as she had been calm for so many months.

Mrs Dashwood was delighted when she heard the news, and she hugged Edward and Elinor with tears in her eyes. Edward said that he would be a clergyman at Delaford, and that his income would be small but enough.
Colonel Brandon came to visit Barton Cottage very often, and he was always gentle and kind. Marianne noticed his quiet goodness for the first time, and she began to enjoy his company.
Edward and Elinor married in the autumn, and they moved into the parsonage at Delaford. It was a small house with a garden, and they were happy there, even though they had very little money.
Willoughby married his rich wife, but he was never truly happy, because he often thought about Marianne. He regretted what he had done for the rest of his life, though he found other pleasures.

At nineteen, Marianne found herself marrying Colonel Brandon, which she would have found impossible two years earlier. She grew to love him as deeply as she had once loved Willoughby, and she was the pride of Delaford.

The two sisters lived within sight of each other for the rest of their lives, and they were always the best of friends. Elinor had learned to share her feelings, and Marianne had learned to control hers.
C1C2: When Mr Henry Dashwood fell gravely ill, he knew that the law would give Norland Park to his son John, the child of his first marriage, and leave his second wife and three daughters with very little. On his deathbed he begged John to protect them and make them comfortable, and John, who was a decent if weak young man, solemnly promised that he would. Within a few days the old man was gone, and the family's fortunes depended wholly on a promise.

At first John thought that he might give his three half sisters a gift of three thousand pounds, which was a generous sum and one that his conscience approved. But his wife Fanny, who was selfish and clever, argued that the girls were quite poor enough already, that their mother could manage on very little, and that charity began at home. By the end of one long conversation, the gift had shrunk to nothing, and John felt no shame at all.

Elinor, the eldest, had a strong understanding and a calm heart, and she had learned to govern her feelings and to think before speaking. Marianne, her sister, was generous, eager and romantic in everything, and she despised any display of coldness or restraint as a kind of falsehood. Their mother loved both, and found it hard to say which of the two she should worry about more.

Soon after the funeral, John and Fanny arrived at Norland Park with their little son, and Fanny at once behaved as though the house had always been hers. She spoke to Mrs Dashwood with chilly politeness, remarked on how large the family was, and hinted that the Dashwoods might soon wish to find a home of their own. Mrs Dashwood, who was proud as well as sensitive, wished to leave at once, but there seemed to be nowhere to go.

Among Fanny's visitors was her brother Edward Ferrars, a shy, gentle young man who showed none of the show and ambition that his family expected of him. He and Elinor spent long hours together in quiet conversation, and she came to value his honest heart and sensible mind above any brilliance. Fanny, who had grander plans for her brother's future, saw the friendship and disliked it intensely.

At the very moment when the family's discomfort was greatest, a letter came from a cousin of Mrs Dashwood's, Sir John Middleton, who lived in Devonshire. He offered her a small cottage on his estate, at a modest rent, and wrote with such warmth that she decided to accept it immediately. It was far from Norland, and far from Edward, but she could no longer bear to stay.

After a sorrowful parting from Norland, in which Marianne wept over every tree, the Dashwoods travelled to their new home in Devonshire. Barton Cottage was small and rather plain, with low ceilings and narrow rooms, but it stood in the middle of a green valley where the hills rose in handsome slopes. Mrs Dashwood, a lady of lively hopes, declared that a little ingenuity could make it charming.

Sir John Middleton, a cheerful and generous sportsman who delighted in company, called at the cottage at once and invited the family to dine at Barton Park. There the Dashwoods met his elegant but silent wife, Lady Middleton, and her mother, Mrs Jennings, a loud and merry widow who adored gossip and nothing so much as the prospect of a wedding. Within an hour she had decided which of the sisters would marry which gentleman.

At Barton Park they also met Colonel Brandon, a grave and gentleman-like officer of about thirty-five, who was Sir John's close friend. He alone of the company listened to Marianne's music with real attention and feeling, and he seemed to look at her with an expression of sad interest. Marianne, who was not yet seventeen, regarded him as a mere old bachelor who could never again know the joys of romantic love.

One wet morning, Marianne and Margaret went walking on the hills, and as they hurried down the slope in the rain, Marianne slipped and twisted her ankle. A handsome young man with a gun and two dogs appeared out of nowhere, lifted her in his arms, and carried her all the way home, to the great admiration of her mother. He gave his name as John Willoughby and begged leave to call and ask after her.

Willoughby called at the cottage every day to enquire after the injured ankle, and he soon proved to be as lively and sensitive as Marianne herself. They had read the same poems, admired the same music and shared the same opinions on everything from dancing to dress, and they would talk for hours without a pause. Mrs Dashwood, delighted to see her daughter so happy, thought that she had never seen a more perfect match.

Willoughby begged for a lock of Marianne's hair, and she, who saw no reason to hide her love, cut it for him with laughter and joy. Elinor, who believed in discretion, was uneasy, since no formal engagement had been announced and the gift seemed rather too familiar. She said nothing, however, for she could not bear to damp her sister's happiness, and she hoped that all would be explained in time.

Elinor, increasingly anxious, asked her mother whether Marianne and Willoughby were really engaged, since neither of them had ever said so plainly. Mrs Dashwood, who believed that true love needed no announcement, replied that she was certain of their attachment, and that asking for proofs would offend them both. Elinor was not entirely reassured, but she could not argue against a mother's happy confidence.

Marianne and Willoughby, in their high spirits, made a joke of poor Colonel Brandon's quiet manners and his fear of damp, and they laughed at him whenever he was out of the room. Elinor, who respected the Colonel's good sense and kindness, defended him warmly, and she wondered why her sister was so ready to dislike a man who had done her no harm. The Colonel himself said nothing, though he seemed to hear every word and to bear it with the patience of a man long used to disappointment.

Willoughby, whose generosity knew few bounds, offered Marianne a beautiful horse of her own, and she accepted with delight until Elinor reminded her of the facts. The family could not afford to keep a horse, nor could they afford a groom, and it was hardly proper to take so costly a present from a gentleman who was not her promised husband. Marianne, with tears standing in her eyes, gave way at last and sadly refused the gift, though she did not hide how much it cost her.

A party had been arranged to visit Whitwell, a handsome estate belonging to Colonel Brandon, but just as everyone was ready, a letter was brought to him at the breakfast table. He read it, changed colour, and hurried off to London, apologising and refusing to give any reason, to the great disappointment of the whole company. Mrs Jennings, who loved a secret, cheerfully declared that it must be a matter of the heart and that the Colonel would soon be married.

A few days later Marianne confessed with happy pride that Willoughby had taken her on a private tour of Allenham, the house of his rich old relative Mrs Smith, whom they had never met. Elinor was astonished and told her, as gently as she could, that the visit was improper and that people might begin to talk, but Marianne laughed and said that she had done nothing wrong. Elinor sighed and let the matter go, though she felt a certain unease that she could not quite explain to herself.

One morning Willoughby appeared at the cottage looking wretched and told the family, in broken phrases, that he was obliged to go to London at once, as his aunt Mrs Smith had business for him there. He could not say when he would return, he refused to explain further, and he left without making any declaration. Marianne, abandoned to her grief, wept for hours, while Elinor wondered uneasily what could have changed so quickly.

Not long afterward, Edward Ferrars came to Barton Cottage for a week, and Elinor, who had hoped for much from his visit, saw with disappointment that he was dejected and restless. Marianne noticed on his finger a ring set with a lock of hair, and when she asked whose it was, he blushed and said it was his sister's. Elinor, who had hoped for a moment that it was her own hair, said nothing and did not understand.

Edward left at the end of the week, with a manner that suggested he was quite as unhappy to go as they were to lose him. Elinor, who did not wish to add to her mother's anxieties, took up her drawing and her sewing with great determination and refused to speak of her own feelings. Marianne, however, observed her sister's stillness and thought it unnatural, and said that Elinor did not feel as deeply as she should.

Soon two new visitors arrived at Barton Park, Lucy and Anne Steele, the poor young cousins of Mrs Jennings, who had come to enjoy a holiday at Sir John's expense. Lucy was pretty, shrewd and constantly flattering, and she seemed anxious to make a friend of Elinor, while Anne chattered on without discretion. Elinor, who did not like Lucy's air of cunning, answered her with polite coolness.

One evening Lucy took Elinor aside and, in a low voice, told her that she had been secretly engaged to Edward Ferrars for four years, ever since he had been her tutor's pupil. She produced a miniature portrait of him as proof, along with a letter in his handwriting, and watched Elinor's face with careful curiosity. Elinor felt her heart sink, but she answered with such composure that Lucy suspected nothing.

Elinor kept the secret faithfully, telling neither her mother nor her sister, though it was a heavy burden to carry alone. She understood at last Edward's low spirits and the ring with its lock of hair, and she began to pity him as well as herself, for he was bound to a woman he did not truly love. In the privacy of her own room she cried a good deal, but in company she smiled, talked and attended to every kindness expected of her.

That winter, the good-natured Mrs Jennings invited the two eldest Miss Dashwoods to accompany her to London, and Mrs Dashwood, hoping that a change would be good for them both, accepted on their behalf. Marianne agreed with feverish eagerness, having no thought but that she might meet Willoughby again, while Elinor went chiefly out of love for her sister. Neither of them expected that the journey would change both of their lives so thoroughly, or that it would cost them so much pain.

Within hours of arriving in London, Marianne wrote to Willoughby to tell him where she was staying, and she wrote again on the next day and the day after. No answer came to any of her notes, and every knock at the door made her start, and each disappointment left her paler and more silent. Elinor, who saw her sister grow thin, did not dare to ask what had happened.

At a crowded party, Marianne caught sight of Willoughby standing among the guests with a fashionable young lady on his arm, and she hurried toward him with a face full of joy. He turned and gave her a short, cold bow, spoke a few words to her as if she were a distant acquaintance, and moved quickly away. Marianne, struck dumb with horror and shame, nearly fell where she stood, and Elinor led her gently from the room before anyone could stare.

Next morning there came a short, heartless note, in which Willoughby claimed that he had never meant to give her any hope, and with it came all her letters and the precious lock of hair. Elinor soon learned that he was engaged to marry a rich young heiress named Miss Grey, and had chosen money over the girl who had loved him. Marianne, in utter misery, lay on the sofa and would speak to no one.

Mrs Jennings, who had a loud voice but a very tender heart, treated the stricken Marianne with kindness, bringing her sweets, wine, and every comfort that her own sorrows had taught her. Her noisy sympathy was exactly what Marianne could not bear, and the girl shrank from every word, but Elinor saw that this vulgar old lady was more kindly than many a polished one. She thanked her warmly for all her care and begged her to be patient with a girl who could not yet bear to be consoled.

Colonel Brandon called at the house and, after some hesitation, told Elinor the true story of Willoughby, speaking in a low and troubled voice. In his youth he had loved a young woman who had died, leaving a little daughter named Eliza Williams in his care, and Willoughby, he said, had seduced the girl, left her with a child, and never once offered help. It was the news in his letter, he explained, that had called him away so suddenly from Whitwell.

Elinor decided that her sister must be told, and so, with gentle care, she repeated all that the Colonel had said, leaving out nothing of importance. Marianne listened in silence, wept a good deal, and began very slowly to understand that the Willoughby whom she had worshipped had never truly existed. It was a bitter lesson, and it did something to her that no kindness had yet been able to achieve.

John and Fanny Dashwood arrived in London that season, and Fanny, who knew nothing of Lucy's secret, took a fancy to the pretty Miss Steele and invited both sisters to stay at her house. She would have been appalled to learn that Lucy was engaged to her own brother, and Elinor, who did know, watched in a silence that was more painful than any outburst. The weeks passed in this way, with a great many bitter little ironies that Elinor alone was able to taste.

Anne Steele, who had never kept a secret in her life, blurted out the whole story of Lucy's engagement to Fanny, who was seized by hysterics at once. Mrs Ferrars, summoned in haste, flew into a violent rage at the thought of her son marrying a girl with neither money nor connections, and the poor Steele sisters were turned out of the house in disgrace. The whole house rang with accusations and tears, and nobody had a calm word for anyone else for the rest of the afternoon.

Mrs Ferrars summoned Edward and demanded that he break his engagement at once, promising to make him rich if he obeyed and ruin him if he did not. Edward, who had been weak in many things, was firm in this, and he said that he had given his word and would keep it, whatever the cost. His mother disinherited him on the spot and gave the whole fortune to his younger brother Robert.

Colonel Brandon, who admired the honour with which Edward had behaved, offered him the living of Delaford, a small parish with a decent house and a modest but sufficient income. He asked Elinor to carry the message, since he scarcely knew the young man himself, and she accepted the task with perfect composure, although it meant helping the man she loved to marry another woman. Edward, when he was told, was touched almost to speechlessness, and he never forgot who had first thought of him.

In the spring Elinor and Marianne at last left London, and on their way home they stopped at Cleveland, the country house of Mrs Jennings's daughter, Mrs Palmer, and her cheerfully sarcastic husband. The house was large and comfortable, with a fine garden, and Marianne, who found it the only quiet place where she could think, spent most of her time walking alone among the trees. Elinor was glad to see her out of doors, though she was still pale and thin.

One evening Marianne walked among the wet grass of the Cleveland garden until dark, indulging the memory of Willoughby and not noticing that her feet and her dress were soaked. She went to bed feverish, with a cold that quickly became a serious illness, and within two days she was delirious and weak, hardly knowing her own sister. Elinor, who stayed up for night after night to nurse her, felt a growing dread.

As the fever grew worse, Elinor sat by her sister's bed through the long nights, and the doctor, Mr Harris, shook his head and said nothing hopeful. Colonel Brandon, who happened to be visiting Cleveland, immediately offered to fetch Mrs Dashwood from Barton, and set off in the middle of the night with a haste that expressed all his anxiety. Elinor was grateful beyond words for such quick and silent kindness, and she began to see in him a depth of goodness that few had noticed.

That night, as Marianne's fever reached its crisis, Willoughby arrived at Cleveland, having heard from a friend that she was dying, and begged to speak with Elinor. He confessed that he had loved Marianne truly, but that his aunt, learning of his wickedness toward Eliza Williams, had cast him off, and that fear of poverty had driven him to marry for money. Elinor listened with pity and with anger, and gave him no promise of forgiveness.

Toward morning the fever broke, and Marianne sank into a deep and natural sleep, and Mr Harris pronounced that all danger was past. Mrs Dashwood, arriving with the Colonel just as the sun was rising, was greeted at the door by the news that her daughter would live, and she wept with a joy that was almost too great to bear. Elinor, exhausted, accepted her mother's embrace and slept for the first time in days.

When Marianne was strong enough to listen, Elinor told her all that Willoughby had said at Cleveland, softening only what would give needless pain. Marianne wept, and then she thought for a long while, and at last she admitted that her own wild feelings had carried her to the edge of a precipice, and that she had nearly died of her own heedlessness. She said that she would henceforth learn to govern herself, and that from that day forward she would try to be more like her sister.

Back at Barton Cottage, Marianne drew up a strict plan of improvement, resolving to read for six hours a day and to practise her music with new discipline. She also thanked Elinor warmly for her patience and her example, which she now saw to have been her own best chance of safety, and she declared that she would never again allow her feelings to rule her. Elinor smiled, thanked her, and did not tell her that so strict a plan was perhaps another kind of extreme, which time would soften.

One afternoon a servant returned from Exeter with the startling news that he had met Mr Ferrars, and that Mr Ferrars's new wife, formerly Miss Steele, had been with him. Elinor, who had been bracing herself for this announcement for months, nevertheless felt her heart go cold and left the room before anyone could see her face. For some time she walked alone in the garden, trying to compose her thoughts.

A few days later, to Elinor's astonishment, Edward Ferrars himself rode up to the gate of the cottage, looking pale and anxious and quite unlike a married man. In a trembling voice he explained that the new Mrs Ferrars was Lucy, who had abandoned him for his richer brother Robert, and that he himself, after four years of captivity, was now entirely free. Elinor had to leave the room to hide her tears of joy, and it was some time before she could trust herself to return.

When he found Elinor alone, Edward told her honestly that he had never loved Lucy, that he had been foolish and young, and that his heart had always been hers. He asked her to marry him, in spite of his poverty and the loss of his fortune, and Elinor, whose long composure at last gave way, said yes through tears of happiness. It was the first time in months that she had wept for joy instead of sorrow.

Mrs Dashwood, who had loved Edward for years, was overcome with delight, and she embraced him and Elinor with tears running down her face. Edward explained that he meant to take holy orders and accept the living of Delaford, that his income would be small but sufficient, and that he would be perfectly content to live modestly with the woman he loved. Elinor looked at him with undisguised pride, for she knew how much that quiet decision had cost him, and how willingly he had paid.

Colonel Brandon, whose attachment had never wavered, came often to Barton Cottage, and Marianne, recovered in health and wiser in heart, found for the first time how much she valued his company. He listened to her music as before, but she now noticed the courage, the integrity and the patience behind his grave manner, qualities for which she had been blind in her brighter days. His long and patient kindness had, after so many disappointments, at last found a way into her heart, and she did not wish to shut it out.

Edward and Elinor were married quietly that autumn, and they settled in the parsonage at Delaford, a small, snug house with a garden of roses and a view of the hills. Their income was modest, but Mrs Ferrars, who had in the end made peace with her son, gave them a gift of money to start with, and they were happier than they could have imagined. Elinor, who had been so strong, at last allowed herself to be taken care of.

Willoughby married his heiress and lived comfortably enough, with a handsome fortune and a good deal of sport, yet he was never wholly happy. He thought of Marianne often, and when he heard of her marriage, he was uneasy for many days, though he took comfort in his horses and his dogs. It was a modest punishment, though it was a real one, and he was left to bear it for the rest of his comfortable life.

At nineteen, Marianne found herself, to her own astonishment, a bride at the altar, about to marry a man whom she had once thought too old to be loved. She now saw in the Colonel all that she had missed in her youth, a good man and a faithful friend, and she gave him her whole heart as completely as she had once given it to Willoughby. Together they made Delaford a place of kindness, comfort and good company, where every neighbour was received with a warm welcome.

Elinor and Marianne lived within sight of each other for the rest of their lives, and their friendship, which had survived so many trials, was never disturbed again. The elder sister had learned that sense need not mean silence, and the younger that sensibility needed the guidance of judgement, and each had been improved by what the other taught her. At Delaford, the old stories of Norland, Barton and Cleveland were told and retold with much laughter.
